chapter: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
title: Playing drums half and half; left-handed musicians
summary: He explains his unusual right-footed, left-handed setup and they note left-handed players like Sharkey and Ray Lopez.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: I was going to ask you about your cornet. You play the cornet, though, right-handed, don't you?
Yeah. Yeah. Well, I play drums half and half. I don't play left-handed drums.

I play half and half. I play right-footed and left-handed. See, I originally started all left. See? And then, I don't know, it was more, my right leg was better. I could keep better time with the right leg than I could with the left. And then you didn't, we didn't have those flying horse things then, you know. And so I got, I don't know how I ever did it. Just all of a sudden I changed and put the, instead of putting the snare drum over on the left where it's supposed to be, I put it on the right so I could have the right leg free, you see. And that's how I got started to play. I've had more drummers, you know, come in and look up like Krupa or Buddy Rich and those guys coming, they look up there and they're trying to figure out what I was doing, you know. You can't figure it out. The guy played half and half, you know.
But the cornet, I do a lot of things right-handed. I eat right-handed. There's only a couple of things that I got to do left-handed.
What about Sharky? Of course we can ask him too, we haven't interviewed him, but he plays fingers at left-handed.
Yeah. Kikla Rocca used to, I guess Ray Lopez.
Left-handed. I just wondered if some of those fellas.
There was another guy around here, Vega. Lawrence Vega, I think his name was, he played left-handed too. Yeah.
I just wondered if some of those fellas maybe weren't left-handed and just thought that was the way to do it because they saw somebody else.
